blocks.content: Left join covered keeping every row from the left table, matched or not. Right join is the mirror image of that same idea, keeping every row from the right table instead, regardless of whether a genuine match exists on the left side.

This topic covers exactly what a right join keeps, a worked example using orphaned orders, finding unmatched rows on the right side, and why right join is rarely actually written in practice compared to left join.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784364087552-336470878.png
blocks.alt: Right join keeps every row from the right table instead, the mirror image of left join

blocks.content: 1. What a Right Join Actually Keeps
blocks.text: 1. What a Right Join Actually Keeps

blocks.content: A right join genuinely keeps every row from the right table in the query, regardless of whether a matching row exists on the left side. When no genuine match exists, the columns coming from the left table simply become NULL for that row.
This means the right table is treated the same way the left table was treated in a left join, kept completely, while the left table is only included where a real match actually exists.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784364089444-714957675.png
blocks.alt: A right join keeps every row from the right table; unmatched rows get NULL values for the left table columns

blocks.content: 2. Right Join Compared To Left Join
blocks.text: 2. Right Join Compared To Left Join

blocks.content: A right join and a left join produce the exact same result whenever the table order is simply swapped. Writing customers RIGHT JOIN orders genuinely returns the same rows as writing orders LEFT JOIN customers, just with the columns listed in a different order.
Because of this, right join and left join are not two independently necessary tools. They are the same underlying operation, described from two different starting points.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784364091010-753592626.png
blocks.alt: Right join and left join produce the same result when the table order is swapped between them

3. A Worked Example

Suppose the orders table has a few rows with a customer_id that no longer matches any real row in customers, perhaps because a customer account was genuinely deleted after placing an order. A right join surfaces those orphaned orders instead of silently dropping them.

Every row from orders appears in this result, matched or not. An order placed by a since deleted customer still appears, with c.name showing NULL, since no genuinely matching customer row exists anymore.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784364093364-854530177.png
blocks.alt: A worked example: right joining orders against customers surfaces orphaned orders with a NULL customer name

blocks.content: 4. Finding Unmatched Rows On The Right Side
blocks.text: 4. Finding Unmatched Rows On The Right Side

blocks.content: The same NULL check pattern from left join applies here, just pointed at the other table. Filtering on a left side column being NULL after a right join isolates exactly the right side rows with no genuine match.

SELECT o.id, o.amount
FROM customers c
RIGHT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id=c.id
WHERE c.id IS NULL;
blocks.code:
SELECT o.id, o.amount
FROM customers c
RIGHT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id=c.id
WHERE c.id IS NULL;

codes.sql:
SELECT o.id, o.amount
FROM customers c
RIGHT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id=c.id
WHERE c.id IS NULL;

blocks.content: This query returns only orphaned orders, rows in the orders table with no genuinely valid matching customer at all, which is a genuinely useful way to audit data integrity issues after the fact.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784364095291-940193286.png
blocks.alt: Filtering on a NULL left side column after a right join isolates unmatched rows on the right side

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: The IS NULL check must target a column from the side that can genuinely go missing, the left table in a right join. Checking a right side column instead defeats the entire point of the filter.
5. Why Right Join Is Rarely Actually Used
blocks.text: 5. Why Right Join Is Rarely Actually Used

blocks.content: Because right join and left join are interchangeable by simply reordering the tables, most teams standardize on left join alone and never write RIGHT JOIN directly. Reading one consistent join direction across an entire codebase is genuinely easier than mentally flipping direction per query.
This is a real, common style convention, not a technical requirement. A right join is not wrong to write, it is just rarely the convention a team actually settles on.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784364098980-502710064.png
blocks.alt: Right join is rarely written directly since reordering tables turns it into an equivalent left join

blocks.title: Worth remembering
blocks.content: If a query reviewer asks you to rewrite a right join as a left join, they are almost always asking for a style change, not a correctness fix. Both forms return the exact same rows.
6. Genuinely Common Mistakes

A few real patterns undermine right join usage. Assuming the left table stays complete instead of the right table, which is backward from what a right join actually does. Mixing right join and left join within a single long query, which makes the real matching logic genuinely hard to follow.
And forgetting the ON clause entirely, which produces the same uncontrolled row combination problem a right join shares with every other join type.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784364101135-50762712.png
blocks.alt: Common mistakes: confusing which side stays complete, mixing join directions, and forgetting the ON clause
